Distinct from holy basil/tulsi (Ocimum tenuiflorum).
references: Educational culinary-herbal and Mediterranean folk sources; folklore only, not medical advice.

latin: Amaranthus spp. (e.g. Amaranthus hypochondriacus, A. cruentus)
cautionsNote: Leaves and seeds are foods. Leaves (like spinach/chard) contain oxalates and can accumulate nitrates if heavily fertilized, so very large quantities of raw leaf are best avoided by those prone to kidney stones. Seeds should be cooked. No notable drug interactions in food use.
references: Educational ethnobotanical and folk-medicine sources of the Americas and Africa; folklore only, not medical advice.

cautionsNote: A common vegetable. Traditionally regarded as a gentle diuretic, so caution is advised in the rare case of medically restricted fluids; ample water should accompany diuretic use. Contact allergy/rash is possible in sensitive individuals. Note: garden asparagus is distinct from Asparagus racemosus (Shatavari).
references: Educational European herbal and dietary sources (e.g. Commission E for the herb as a diuretic); folklore only, not medical advice.

cautionsNote: Needle infusion is a traditional vitamin-C-rich respiratory tea. Correct identification is essential: yew (Taxus) and some other conifers are toxic and not true pines, and several sources advise pregnant women avoid pine-needle preparations. Pine essential oil/turpentine is for external/diffused use only, can irritate skin and airways, and must not be ingested.
references: Educational Northern-Hemisphere folk and wildcraft sources; folklore only, not medical advice. Identification critical (avoid toxic look-alikes such as yew).

cautionsNote: Pungent mustard-oil glycosides may irritate the stomach in large amounts or aggravate existing gastric/kidney irritation; generally regarded as a safe edible. Educational folklore, not medical advice.
references: Traditional European herbal use; modern educational herbals on Tropaeolum majus as a natural antibiotic-type herb. Educational only.

cautionsNote: Cassia cinnamon (C. cassia) is high in coumarin, which can stress the liver in large/long-term doses and may interact with anticoagulants; Ceylon cinnamon (C. verum) is much lower in coumarin. Concentrated cinnamon oil is a mucous-membrane irritant. May affect blood sugar (interaction with diabetes medication). Therapeutic doses traditionally cautioned in pregnancy. Educational folklore, not medical advice.
references: Long-standing culinary and traditional use across South/East Asia and Europe; educational food-science references on coumarin content. Educational only.

cautionsNote: Concentrated clove (eugenol) oil is potent: undiluted it can irritate or burn skin and oral mucosa, and ingestion of the oil can be toxic, especially to children and the liver. Eugenol may slow blood clotting (interaction with anticoagulants). Culinary amounts of the whole spice are considered safe. Educational folklore, not medical advice.
references: Traditional dental and digestive folk use; widely documented eugenol pharmacology in educational sources. Educational only.

cautionsNote: Leaf is widely used as a nutritious food; however the root, root bark and their extracts contain alkaloids (e.g. spirochin) and are traditionally avoided, especially in pregnancy, as they have been associated with uterine activity and can be toxic. Educational folklore, not medical advice.
references: Traditional South Asian food and Ayurvedic use; educational nutrition literature on Moringa oleifera leaf. Educational only.

cautionsNote: A revered Ayurvedic herb generally well tolerated as a tea. Some traditional and educational sources advise caution in pregnancy and when trying to conceive (possible anti-fertility effects in animal studies, attributed to ursolic acid), and it may add to the effect of blood-thinning or blood-sugar-lowering medication. Educational folklore, not medical advice.
references: Ayurvedic tradition (revered as a sacred plant); educational adaptogen and herbal references on Ocimum tenuiflorum / O. sanctum. Educational only.

cautionsNote: Comfrey contains hepatotoxic pyrrolizidine alkaloids and is NOT recommended for internal use; it can cause serious liver damage. Modern educational guidance restricts it to external use on unbroken skin, in limited amounts and for short periods only, and avoids it in pregnancy/breastfeeding and on open wounds. Traditional name 'knitbone' refers to topical use over closed injuries. Educational folklore, not medical advice.
references: Traditional European wound/bone folk medicine ('knitbone'); educational toxicology on pyrrolizidine alkaloids. Educational only.

cautionsNote: Mainly used externally as an astringent; widely regarded as safe topically. The tannins can be irritating to some skin and, if taken internally in quantity, may upset the stomach; commercial distillates contain little tannin. Educational folklore, not medical advice.
references: Indigenous North American and later Eclectic-physician topical use; educational dermatological-herbal references. Educational only.

cautionsNote: Contains salicylates (salicylaldehyde, methyl salicylate); avoid in people with aspirin/salicylate sensitivity and use caution alongside anticoagulant or antiplatelet medication. Traditionally avoided in those who should not take aspirin (e.g. children with viral fevers).
references: Traditional European herbalism; ESCOP/EMA herbal monographs on Filipendulae ulmariae flos/herba (educational, not medical advice).

origin: South Asia (Western Ghats of India / Sri Lanka, tropical)
cautionsNote: Generally regarded as safe as a culinary spice. Concentrated essential oil should not be ingested undiluted; gallstone sufferers traditionally use medicinal amounts with caution. Possible allergy in sensitive individuals.

references: Ayurvedic and Unani traditional use; culinary ethnobotany (educational, not medical advice).

origin: Central/East Asia (temperate to subtropical); now cultivated worldwide
cautionsNote: Legal status is restricted/regulated in many jurisdictions - check local law. Psychoactive (THC) can impair driving and cognition, may trigger anxiety or precipitate psychosis in vulnerable people, and is not advised in pregnancy or breastfeeding. Interacts with sedatives and other medications. Hemp seed and seed oil are non-psychoactive foods.
references: Ethnobotany and modern pharmacology of Cannabis; genetic studies point to an East/Central Asian origin; regulatory status varies by country (educational, not medical or legal advice).

latin: Bambusa vulgaris (and related genera, subfamily Bambusoideae)
origin: Tropical and subtropical Asia (also Africa and the Americas)
cautionsNote: Fresh raw shoots of many species contain cyanogenic (taxiphyllin) compounds and must be boiled before eating; the silica-rich 'tabasheer' and leaf preparations are traditional, not a substitute for medical care. Identify species carefully.
references: Traditional Asian use (esp. Chinese 'zhu ru' / tabasheer) and ethnobotany (educational, not medical advice).

cautionsNote: Primarily used topically/externally. Neem oil and concentrated extracts taken internally can be toxic - neem oil ingestion has caused serious poisoning (Reye-like syndrome) especially in infants and children, who should not be given it. Avoid internal use in pregnancy (traditionally regarded as abortifacient) and breastfeeding; may affect blood sugar and interact with medications.
references: Ayurvedic and folk use across South Asia; toxicology literature on neem oil (educational, not medical advice).

cautionsNote: Generally very safe as a food and cosmetic oil; rare nut/seed-oil allergy is possible, and the cosmetic and culinary (roasted) oils are distinct grades. Conservation note: the argan tree is assessed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List - choose oil from sustainable, fair-trade sources that support the Moroccan arganeraie.
references: Moroccan (Amazigh/Berber) traditional use and cosmetic science; IUCN Red List assessment of Argania spinosa / Sideroxylon spinosum, Vulnerable (educational, not medical advice).

origin: Western Asia, Middle East and Southern Europe (Mediterranean to South Asia)
cautionsNote: Culinary seed amounts are well established; concentrated oil/extract in large doses may lower blood pressure and blood sugar and could interact with anticoagulants, antihypertensives and diabetes medication. Large medicinal doses are traditionally avoided in pregnancy. Undiluted essential oil should not be ingested.
references: Unani, Ayurvedic and Middle Eastern traditional use; modern phytochemistry of thymoquinone (educational, not medical advice).

cautionsNote: Seed oil (a source of gamma-linolenic acid, GLA) may interact with anticoagulant and antiplatelet medications and may lower the seizure threshold; caution with anticonvulsants. Traditionally avoided in pregnancy as a precaution. Educational folklore, not medical advice.
conservationStatus_verified: Common; widespread weedy biennial, no conservation concern.
references: Educational/traditional herbal sources (e.g. monographs on Oenothera biennis seed oil and GLA). Folklore, not medical advice. Origin and constituents verified against botanical monographs.

cautionsNote: Traditionally regarded as mildly sedating and mood-altering; the alkaloids nuciferine and apomorphine are the usual attribution, though analyses show these can be low or absent in many commercial products. May add to the effects of sedatives/alcohol; avoid before driving. Not for use in pregnancy. Educational folklore, not medical advice.
references: Ethnobotanical/educational sources on ancient Egyptian use of Nymphaea caerulea. Native to the Nile region of North/East Africa, NOT South Africa. Alkaloid content verified against published GC-MS analyses. Folklore, not medical advice.

cautionsNote: Generally well tolerated as a food with a long history of dietary use. Fruit pulp is high in fibre and vitamin C; very large amounts may cause digestive upset. Educational folklore, not medical advice.
references: African ethnobotanical and food/educational sources on Adansonia digitata. Native across mainland sub-Saharan Africa (iconic savanna tree); present in southern Africa but NOT exclusively South African. IUCN: Least Concern. Folklore, not medical advice.

cautionsNote: Caffeine is a stimulant: can cause insomnia, anxiety, palpitations and raised blood pressure, and may interact with various medications. Pregnant and breastfeeding people are advised to limit intake. Educational folklore, not medical advice.
references: Botanical/educational sources on Coffea arabica and caffeine. Coffea arabica originates in the Ethiopian highlands (East Africa). Folklore, not medical advice.

cautionsNote: Contains theobromine and some caffeine (mild stimulants) plus tyramine-related compounds; rich in oxalates. Large amounts may cause restlessness or, with high oxalate intake, contribute to kidney-stone risk in susceptible people; may interact with MAOI medications. Theobromine is toxic to dogs and other pets. Educational folklore, not medical advice.
references: Botanical/ethnobotanical sources on Theobroma cacao and Mesoamerican use. Native to the tropical Americas (Amazon basin), domesticated in Mesoamerica. NOTE: cacao is a mild stimulant, not a sedative; 'sedating' caution removed as inaccurate. Folklore, not medical advice.

cautionsNote: Leaves and flowers contain small amounts of pyrrolizidine alkaloids that can be harmful to the liver, so the herb is not recommended for prolonged internal use, in pregnancy, or while breastfeeding. Seed oil (a GLA source) may interact with anticoagulant/antiplatelet drugs and lower the seizure threshold. Educational folklore, not medical advice.
references: Traditional/educational herbal sources on Borago officinalis. Native to the Mediterranean region; widely naturalised in temperate gardens. Pyrrolizidine-alkaloid hepatotoxicity verified against herbal pharmacovigilance literature. Folklore, not medical advice.

cautionsNote: The latex contains morphine, codeine and related opiate alkaloids: highly sedating, addictive and potentially fatal in overdose (respiratory depression). Cultivation and use of the latex/opium are legally controlled in most countries. The culinary seeds contain only trace alkaloids but can still affect drug tests. This is strictly educational folklore and history, NOT medical advice or a how-to.
references: Botanical/historical and pharmacognosy educational sources on Papaver somniferum. Native to the eastern Mediterranean and Western Asia; cultivated since antiquity. Presented as history, not guidance. Educational/historical only, not medical advice.

cautionsNote: Asteraceae-family allergen (cross-reactivity with ragweed/daisies); concentrated preparations and essential oil traditionally avoided in pregnancy. Educational folklore, not medical advice.
constituents: volatile oil (angelic and tiglic acid esters)
references: Educational herbal/botanical references (e.g. Grieve's A Modern Herbal; ESCOP/EMA Matricaria & Chamaemelum monographs). Folklore only.

cautionsNote: Seeds/concentrated extracts traditionally avoided in pregnancy (uterine stimulant in folklore). Contains furocoumarins (psoralens) that can cause phototoxic skin reactions; recognised food allergen; theoretical interaction with diuretics/anticoagulants. Educational folklore, not medical advice.
references: Educational botanical/herbal references (e.g. Grieve's A Modern Herbal; standard materia medica). Folklore only.

origin: Central Asia / Siberia (Rheum genus); medicinal Chinese rhubarb (Rheum palmatum) from western China
cautionsNote: LEAVES ARE TOXIC and must never be eaten (high oxalic acid / anthraquinones); only the petiole (stalk) is a food. Root is a stimulant laxative (anthraquinones) — not for prolonged use, in pregnancy/breastfeeding, or with bowel obstruction; can interact with certain medications. Educational folklore, not medical advice.
references: Educational botanical/herbal references (e.g. Grieve's A Modern Herbal; traditional Chinese materia medica for Da Huang). Folklore only.

origin: Tropical Americas (Andean South America / Central America)
cautionsNote: HIGHLY TOXIC and addictive — nicotine is a potent poison; not for internal/medicinal use. Listed here for its ethnobotanical and ritual-spiritual role among Indigenous American peoples (sacred plant, ceremonial smoke/offering) and historical use as a botanical insecticide. Smoking causes serious harm. Educational/ethnobotanical context only, NEVER medical advice.
references: Ethnobotanical literature on Indigenous American sacred-plant use; standard toxicology. Educational context only, not a remedy.

cautionsNote: Generally regarded as a gentle culinary herb; classic folk 'gripe water' carminative for infant colic. Apiaceae-family allergen for sensitive individuals; concentrated seed/essential-oil doses beyond culinary amounts are not advised in pregnancy. Educational folklore, not medical advice.
references: Educational herbal/botanical references (e.g. Grieve's A Modern Herbal; EMA Anethum monograph). Folklore only.

cautionsNote: Widely used culinary and carminative herb; recognised food allergen for some (can cause contact/oral allergy). Concentrated seed extracts/essential oil beyond culinary amounts not advised in pregnancy. Educational folklore, not medical advice.
references: Educational herbal/botanical references (e.g. Grieve's A Modern Herbal; EMA Coriandrum monograph). Folklore only.

origin: Eurasia (Siberia / Central Asia), also native to western North America
cautionsNote: Culinary herb (French tarragon) used as a digestive bitter and appetite stimulant. The essential oil is high in estragole (methylchavicol) and can also contain methyleugenol — both genotoxic carcinogens in concentrated form — so medicinal-strength/long-term internal use and the neat essential oil are avoided in pregnancy and not for prolonged use. Asteraceae-family allergen. (Trace beta-thujone may occur in some chemotypes, but estragole is the defining concern, not thujone.) Educational folklore, not medical advice.
references: Educational herbal/botanical references (e.g. Grieve's A Modern Herbal; standard materia medica on Artemisia; phytochemical surveys of A. dracunculus essential-oil chemotypes). Folklore only.

cautionsNote: Culinary amounts are considered safe in food. Avoid medicinal/concentrated doses (especially seed and seed oil, which contains apiole/myristicin) during pregnancy as it may stimulate the uterus. Large or concentrated amounts (e.g. parsley juice) are a traditional anti-galactagogue and may reduce milk supply when breastfeeding. Furanocoumarins can cause photosensitivity on skin contact with sun. May interact with anticoagulants (warfarin) due to vitamin K content, and theoretically with diuretics.
references: Traditional European herbalism and culinary use; folklore/educational only, not medical advice.

cautionsNote: Culinary flower buds (capers) are typically brine- or salt-cured and eaten in small amounts; the high salt content of cured capers is a consideration for those limiting sodium or managing blood pressure. Traditional medicinal use of root bark is folkloric. Possible allergic reaction in sensitive individuals.
references: Traditional Mediterranean herbalism and culinary use; folklore/educational only, not medical advice.
